passage:
Playgroup teacher's note, after Mishti's birthday party.
Kashish arrived holding her mother Seema's dupatta and stayed behind her legs. An aunty bent down: "Say hello! Don't be shy!" Kashish pressed her face into the dupatta and went completely still.
I asked the aunty to give her time. Seema sat on the floor near the blocks, and Kashish sat on her lap, watching the others build.
After a long while she whispered to me, "Can I put the red one?" I nodded. By cake time she was building next to Mishti, still quiet.
Next week in class I will seat her near the block corner, and let her join when she is ready.

qa.q: What was Kashish holding when she arrived?
qa.a: Her mother Seema's dupatta.

qa.q: How did Kashish feel when the aunty told her to say hello?
qa.a: She felt shy and frozen; she pressed her face into the dupatta and went completely still.

qa.q: What helped Kashish join in, according to the teacher's note?
qa.a: Being given time, sitting on Seema's lap near the blocks to watch first, and a simple nod when she whispered to join.

qa.q: How might the aunty see Kashish's silence, and what would change if she waited?
qa.a: The aunty may think Kashish is being rude or just shy; if she waited, Kashish could warm up at her own pace instead of freezing.

grounding: Shows a slow-to-warm child who hides behind her mother, whispers, and joins play after watching, and how pushing to say hello deepens the freeze.

subtype: Wanting to join but holding back [Actor]
passage:
Every evening the colony kids played seven stones in the lane behind Block C. Ganga watched from the steps with her chin on her knees.
She knew the rules by heart. She even knew Pinky always aimed too high. But what if she asked and they said no? What if she threw and missed everything?
On Thursday the ball rolled right to her feet. She held it, heart thumping.
Harish jogged over. "Good catch. You want to play? We need one more on our side."
Ganga nodded, cheeks hot. Her first throw missed. Harish just said, "Next one."
Her second throw knocked down three stones. Nobody made a big fuss. They just yelled, "Run!" and she ran.
The next evening, she walked straight down from the steps.

qa.q: Where did the colony kids play seven stones?
qa.a: In the lane behind Block C.

qa.q: What was Ganga worried about while she watched?
qa.a: She felt anxious that they would say no if she asked, or that she would throw and miss everything.

qa.q: What did Harish do that made it easier for Ganga to join?
qa.a: He invited her with a simple reason, "We need one more on our side," and when she missed he just said "Next one" instead of teasing.

qa.q: What would change if nobody had invited Ganga?
qa.a: She might have kept watching from the steps, longing to play but waiting, and her worry about saying or doing the wrong thing could have grown.

grounding: Shows a child who longs to join a game but waits to be invited, and how a peer's friendly bridge and a safe try ease her shyness.

passage:
"This is Devika, she's our shy one," her mother told the new art teacher on the first day. Devika had heard it at every family function, at the tailor's, at the bus stop. Lately she'd started saying it herself: "I can't, I'm shy."
The teacher, Ganga Ma'am, only smiled and said, "Hello, Devika."
In class, Ganga Ma'am asked who would pass out the paints. Devika didn't raise her hand, but she stood up when asked. "Thank you, that was helpful."
The next week, Devika showed her painting to the table next to her. Ganga Ma'am noticed. "You shared your work. That took some courage."
At the end of term, Devika raised her hand to explain her own collage. Her voice wobbled, but she finished.

qa.q: What did Devika's mother call her on the first day?
qa.a: She called her "our shy one".

qa.q: How did Devika feel about herself before art class changed things?
qa.a: She felt stuck and small, believing shyness was who she was; she even said, "I can't, I'm shy."

qa.q: Which of Ganga Ma'am's choices helped Devika, and why?
qa.a: Ganga Ma'am never used the shy label and praised each small brave step, like handing out paints and sharing work, so Devika began to feel capable.

qa.q: How might Devika's mother see her differently after the term?
qa.a: Seeing Devika explain her own collage, her mother might notice she can speak up in her own time, not just "our shy one".

grounding: Shows a child who has come to believe the shy label and a teacher who avoids it and praises small brave steps instead.

passage:
Farida Di knocked and came in. "You've been saying the same sentence to the mirror for an hour."
Irawati went red. "I have to ask Sir about the project date tomorrow. What if my voice cracks?"
"Then it cracks. Sir won't notice."
"Everyone will notice." Irawati picked at her sleeve. "I didn't go to the science fair either. Or the debate. I just... couldn't."
"Why not?"
"Because if I say something stupid, they'll remember it forever."
Farida sat on the bed. "Ira, it's not just shyness if it's making you miss things you wanted. The debate, you used to love that."
Irawati's eyes filled. "I know."
"Let's tell Aai tonight, together. And maybe talk to the school counsellor. You don't have to fix this alone."
Irawati nodded, and put down the paper with the sentence on it.

qa.q: What had Irawati skipped besides the debate?
qa.a: She had skipped the science fair.

qa.q: What was Irawati afraid of, and how does it show?
qa.a: She was afraid of being embarrassed and remembered forever for saying something stupid; she rehearsed one sentence for an hour and went red when Farida noticed.

qa.q: What did Farida suggest, and why was it wise?
qa.a: She suggested telling Aai that night and talking to the school counsellor, because the fear was making Irawati miss things she wanted to do.

qa.q: How does Farida see Irawati's avoidance?
qa.a: Farida sees it as more than shyness, because it has taken away things Irawati used to love, like debate, so she wants her to have support.

grounding: Shows a teen whose fear of embarrassment makes her rehearse for hours and skip events, and a cousin who sees it needs support.

passage:
You want to know why I never answer in class? Okay, Nitin, I'll tell you. I'm Ritu, and I know the answers, all right.
But the second Ma'am looks my way, my heart starts pounding, my face goes hot and red, and my head goes totally blank. Like someone switched off a light.
If I do say something, I replay it all evening. The wobble in my voice. The one wrong word. It feels like a disaster.
So I stopped raising my hand. And yes, that felt good at first, such relief. But then the fear got bigger. Now even reading my name on the attendance list feels scary.
Last week I told Ma'am. She said we'd start small: I read one line from my seat, only on days I choose. Yesterday I did it. My heart still pounded. But I got through the line, and nobody laughed.

qa.q: What did Ma'am suggest Ritu do to start?
qa.a: Read one line from Ritu's seat, only on days Ritu chooses.

qa.q: How does Ritu feel after speaking in class, and what shows it?
qa.a: Ritu feels embarrassed and anxious, replaying the wobble and the wrong word all evening as if it were a disaster.

qa.q: Why was telling Ma'am a better step than staying silent?
qa.a: Staying silent brought relief but made the fear bigger; telling Ma'am led to small, chosen steps with help, which let Ritu get through a line.

qa.q: How might Nitin see Ritu differently after hearing this?
qa.a: Nitin might realise Ritu's silence is not lack of knowledge but fear, and could be more patient and encouraging in class.

grounding: Shows a teen whose racing heart and blank mind before speaking lead to avoidance, and how small steps with a teacher's help work better.

passage:
Saturday night
Hemant came to the cricket match today!! First time since Class 8.
I asked on Tuesday, and I said, "No pressure, you can say no." He said maybe. Today he messaged "ok". That's big for him.
At the ground he stood near me the whole time. When Yash asked him something, he looked at me, so I answered the easy part for him, like we'd agreed. He did the second half himself.
I didn't make him bowl. I didn't make a speech about it either. On the way home I just said, "I liked having you there." He smiled at the pavement.
Still, I'm a bit worried. He told me he hasn't been to a family wedding in a year because of the fear, and he cried about missing his cousin's. That's not just being quiet. Tomorrow I'll ask if he'd talk to the school counsellor, or to his mum. I'll offer to go with him.
Gautam

qa.q: Who asked Hemant something at the ground?
qa.a: Yash asked him something.

qa.q: What is Gautam worried about at the end of the diary entry?
qa.a: Gautam feels worried that Hemant's fear is stopping normal life, since he has missed family weddings for a year and cried about his cousin's.

qa.q: What does Gautam do that makes Gautam a supportive friend?
qa.a: Gautam invited Hemant with no pressure, answered only the easy part as they had agreed, didn't make him bowl, and quietly said he liked having him there.

qa.q: What might the day have been like for Hemant?
qa.a: Hemant likely felt nervous but safe staying near Gautam; being noticed kindly, without a fuss, may make it easier for him to come again.

grounding: Shows a teen friend who invites without pressure, speaks for quiet moments as agreed, celebrates small steps, and plans to suggest a counsellor.

passage:
People always ask me, "Why are you so quiet? Are you okay?" And honestly, I'm fine. I'm Dilnaz, second-year botany, and this is just how I am.
At the orientation party I stood near the wall and didn't talk to many people. Someone told me I should "come out of my shell," and I was annoyed, to be honest. I don't live in a shell.
What I like is three or four people, a table, chai, a proper conversation. My friend Maria and I have been talking every Sunday since first year. She knows about my father's shop, my exams, the plant I killed. I know about her sisters. That's worth more to me than fifty people who know my name.
Strangers? I'll warm up, slowly. And if I don't, that's okay too. Quiet isn't the same as unhappy.

qa.q: How often have Dilnaz and Maria been talking since first year?
qa.a: Every Sunday.

qa.q: How did Dilnaz feel when told to "come out of my shell"?
qa.a: Dilnaz felt annoyed, because Dilnaz is fine and does not see being quiet as something wrong.

qa.q: What would you advise someone who wants to help a quiet friend like Dilnaz?
qa.a: Accept that being reserved isn't a problem, and invite them to small, calm meetups rather than pushing them to be more outgoing.

qa.q: How might Maria see Dilnaz's quietness?
qa.a: Maria knows Dilnaz deeply through their Sunday talks, so she likely sees the quiet as part of a loyal, thoughtful friend, not as a problem.

grounding: Shows a young adult who is quiet with strangers, content in small groups, and values a few deep friendships.

passage:
Hostel warden's note, Girls' Block B, October.
Amandeep has missed four seminars this month. Her roommate, Afreen, came to my office on Monday, worried. "She eats alone in the room. She said group work makes her feel like everyone is staring."
I went up that evening. Amandeep was sitting at her desk with a cold plate beside her. She said, "I'm useless at this college. I can't even sit in a room with people." She sounded very alone.
I didn't tell her to just try harder. I said, "It sounds exhausting, and you shouldn't have to carry it by yourself."
What I did next: with her agreement, I called the campus counsellor that same evening, and she has an appointment on Wednesday. I thanked Afreen for telling me. I will check on Amandeep at dinner each day this week.

qa.q: How many seminars has Amandeep missed this month?
qa.a: Four seminars.

qa.q: How was Amandeep feeling when the warden visited?
qa.a: She felt lonely and ashamed of herself, calling herself useless and saying she couldn't even sit in a room with people.

qa.q: Why was calling the counsellor the same evening a wise step?
qa.a: Her avoidance and self-criticism were growing, and getting a counsellor involved early can make a real difference before things build further.

qa.q: What was it like for Afreen to watch Amandeep eat alone?
qa.a: Afreen was worried enough to go to the warden, and may have felt helpless until an adult stepped in.

grounding: Shows a warden seeing a student avoid seminars and meals because being watched feels unbearable, and linking her to a counsellor early.

passage:
Daycare note, Abhinav, Tuesday.
Dropping-off: Abhinav cried hard and reached for his papa, Sahil, when he left. I held him by the window and he settled after a while.
Morning: he toddled to the sand tray, then looked back at me, then went further to the slide. Each time he checked, I smiled.
Pick-up: when Sahil came in, Abhinav ran to him, sobbing again, then snuggled in and was calm in a minute.

qa.q: Where did Abhinav go after the sand tray?
qa.a: He went further to the slide.

qa.q: How did Abhinav feel when his papa left?
qa.a: He was upset and cried hard, reaching for Sahil.

qa.q: Why does the note-writer smile each time Abhinav looks back?
qa.a: The smile tells him the carer is still there, so he feels safe to explore further.

qa.q: What is pick-up like for Sahil?
qa.a: Sahil gets a run and a sob, then a quick snuggle and calm, a sign that Abhinav trusts him to comfort him.

grounding: Shows a toddler who protests at parting, explores while checking back with a carer, and is soothed quickly on his father's return.

subtype: Child who seeks comfort and returns to play [Actor]
passage:
From Pankaj's Amma's notebook, Sunday.
At the park, Pankaj fell off the low wall and scraped his knee. He ran to me shouting "Amma!", crying hard. I held him, blew on the scrape and said, "That hurt, na." Soon his crying slowed. He looked at the knee, then ran back to the swings.
At bedtime he said, "Amma, Rukmini in my class pulls my bag every day. I don't like it."
I thanked him for telling me. Tomorrow I'll speak to his teacher.

qa.q: What happened to Pankaj at the park?
qa.a: He fell off the low wall and scraped his knee.

qa.q: How did Pankaj feel when he fell, and what helped?
qa.a: He was hurt and upset, crying hard, and being held and hearing "That hurt, na" helped him calm down.

qa.q: What did Amma do well at bedtime?
qa.a: She thanked Pankaj for telling her about Rukmini and planned to speak to his teacher, so he learns telling is safe.

qa.q: What would change if Amma had scolded Pankaj for crying at the park?
qa.a: He might learn that showing hurt brings blame, and he might keep problems like the bag-pulling to himself instead of telling her.

grounding: Shows a child who runs to his mother when hurt, is calmed and returns to play, and tells her about a problem without fear of blame.
